lines.say: Here's a puzzle. A gate secretly turns a special state by a fraction of a full turn.
That fraction is called the phase, and in chemistry, it's the number we want.
To read it, picture a clock hand that moves the same secret amount every tick.
Take photos after one, two and four ticks. The four tick photo magnifies tiny differences.
Phase estimation does this with extra counting qubits. Call the hidden fraction phi.
Each counting qubit controls the gate, called U, and phase kickback moves the turn onto it.
Run U once, and the first hand turns by phi. Twice, and the next turns by two phi.
Each doubling slides phi's binary digits one place left, so each qubit sees a finer digit.
Try the S gate, which turns ket one a quarter turn. In binary, a quarter is zero point zero one.
With two counting qubits, one hand turns a quarter, the other twice as far, a half.
The inverse Q F T from the last lesson combines them and reads out zero one, a quarter's digits.
Here the picture breaks. You can't just look at a hand, since measuring gives zero or one.
Only the inverse Q F T can combine those hidden turns into a number.
And the target must be a state that U only turns, called an eigenstate.
Hand it any other state, and you get a random one of U's phases.
So kick U, U twice and U four times onto counting qubits, and the inverse Q F T reads out phi.
